title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
This article is my review of the 2019 paper “A simulation of the insurance industry: The problem of risk model homogeneity” by Heinrich, Sabuco, and Farmer (Heinrich et al. 2021) (released on arXiv in 2019, published in 2021), and my analysis of their simulation of the insurance industry.
The hypothesis of the paper is that if the insurance industry as a whole uses too few catastrophe risk models, many insurers could make correlated underestimates of risk, and there would be a possibility of a large number of insurers going simultaneously bankrupt. This is quite a plausible idea; they bring up Solvency II:

“Under the European regulatory framework Solvency II, insurance companies are required to use only certified risk models. This has led to a situation in which only a few firms provide risk models, creating a systemic fragility to the errors in these models.”

I don’t think this is right? I haven’t been able to find evidence for the claim that only specific catastrophe risk models can be used in calculating a firm’s Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR). If a firm uses an internal model to calculate its SCR, then that internal model (surely containing a cat risk model) will need to be approved by the regulator, but it seems the main issue is that it is very hard to create a good cat risk model, resulting in a lot of concentration in the cat model space.
I admire the ambition of this paper, because it is vast and probably impossible. To have a simulation of the entire insurance industry that is reliable enough to be able to run prospective policy changes on it, and have the results be anything but very weak evidence would be a great achievement. It would have to be extremely nuanced, and if we were going to trust it, we would also need a track record of successful predictions.
As it is then, this paper represents an interesting starting point, and is also interesting to me personally for the following reasons:

I am interested in insurance, and (because it is written in code) a simulation of the insurance industry would have to contain precise statements about how each part of the industry works, so the simulation offers a good learning opportunity.
This is a python project of moderate size. I self taught python and have done a medium sized project myself (a reinforcement learning bridge bot, blog post coming soon), so it would be interesting to see how others do it.

So in this article I:

explore what happens in the simulation and how realistic it seems
explore the approximations/assumptions made by the paper and see if they seem valid

I focus on how the simulation works, not the problem of risk model homogeneity. If someone asked me to give them an analysis of this model of the insurance industry, this is the report I would write.

text:
Insurers
Let’s look at the cash of each insurer over time:

Figure 2





Judging by the uptrending cash lines, most insurers are profitable but eventually leave the market voluntarily. An insurer voluntarily leaves because for a long continuous period it either underwrites hardly any contracts (< 4) or it is barely using its capital (roughly if its cash > 2.5 times its solvency capital requirement) for more than 24 months. (See the MetaInsuranceOrg.market_permanency method).
Let’s enumerate the final states of insurers:

Figure 3





Fraction of voluntary leavers with less than 4 contracts: 5.7%


So:

Most insurers exit despite having lots of underwritten policies
There are always plenty of houses that do not have insurance policies
(By elimination) 94.3% of insurers who leave do so because they are under-utilising their capital

This suggests some kind of flaw in insurer decision making. Perhaps for more realism we could change the simulation so that

Insurers allowed themselves to write policies more quickly they could better use their capital (currently {}{})
Highly profitable insurers paid a higher dividend instead of exiting the market (currently it is always 40% of profit, if there was a profit)

Let’s look at the profitability of insurers (that actually paid some claims):


Code
def log_to_time_series(log):
    # I often coded logs as dictionaries to save memory because many cash flows only occur rarely
    # This function converts them all to arrays for plotting
    t0 = log['start_time']
    tf = log['end_time']
    if tf == None: tf = T
    ts = np.arange(t0, tf+1)
    res = {'ts':ts}
    for k in log.keys():
        d = log[k]
        if k != 'reinrisks_created':
            if type(d) == list:
                res[k] = np.array(d)
            elif type(d) == dict:
                ys = np.zeros(tf-t0+1)
                for t in d.keys():
                    ys[t-t0] = d[t]
                res[k] = ys
        elif k == 'reinrisks_created':
            ys = np.zeros(tf-t0+1)
            for t in d.keys():
                ys[t-t0] = len(d[t])
            res[k] = ys
    return res




Code
net_loss_ratios = []
total_net_claims = 0
total_net_premiums = 0
for insurer in sim.insurancefirms:
    log = insurer.log
    # Ignore firms that were still present at the end, and those that never paid claims
    if log['end_time'] != None and 'claim_out' in log:
        res = log_to_time_series(log)
        if log['dissolution reason'] == 'record_bankruptcy':
            net_claims = sum(res['claim_out']+res['Dissolution_out']-res.get('claim_in',0))
        elif log['dissolution reason'] == 'record_market_exit':
            net_claims = sum(res['claim_out']-res.get('claim_in',0))
        net_premiums = sum(res['premium_in']-res.get('premium_out',0))
        LR = net_claims/net_premiums
        total_net_claims += net_claims
        total_net_premiums += net_premiums
        net_loss_ratios.append(LR)
        assert LR > 0
industry_net_loss_ratio = total_net_claims/total_net_premiums
plt.hist(net_loss_ratios, bins=np.arange(0, max(net_loss_ratios)+0.5, 0.1))
plt.title('Histogram of Insurer Loss Ratios')
plt.xlabel('Count')
plt.ylabel('Loss Ratio')
plt.axvline(1, linestyle='--', color='red')
plt.show()
print(f"Minimum Loss Ratio = {min(net_loss_ratios):0.4f}")
print(f"Mean Loss Ratio = {np.mean(net_loss_ratios):0.3f}")
print(f"Maximum Loss Ratio = {max(net_loss_ratios):0.1f}")
print(f"Fraction of Insurers who are profitable = {np.mean(np.array(net_loss_ratios) < 1):0.3f}")
print(f"Industry Net Loss Ratio = {industry_net_loss_ratio:0.3f}")








Figure 4





Minimum Loss Ratio = 0.0105
Mean Loss Ratio = 0.894
Maximum Loss Ratio = 10.3
Fraction of Insurers who are profitable = 0.754
Industry Net Loss Ratio = 0.729


So most insurers are profitable, but there is a huge variation. The huge loss ratios probably stem from insurers who were hit with a huge catastrophe very soon after entering the market and before securing reinsurance.

Total number of reinsurers founded after end of transient: 72
Number of bankruptcies: 8 = 11%
Number of market exits: 62 = 86%
- of which were immediate market exits: 49 = 68% of total
Number of reinsurers remaining at end: 2 = 2.8%


Like insurers, reinsurers are programmed to exit the market if for a long continuous period (48 time steps for reinsurers) they either have hardly any contracts underwritten (<2) or are barely using their capital (roughly speaking a solvency ratio of over 5).
The following histograms show that reinsurers leave because they are not using enough of their capital, as opposed to not having enough underwritten contracts:


Code
n_contracts = []
cash_utilisation = []
min_reins_lifetime = s['simulation_parameters']["reinsurance_permanency_time_constraint"] # = 48
for reins in sim.reinsurancefirms:
    log = reins.log
    if log['start_time'] >= t_transient and log['end_time'] != None: 
        if log['end_time']+1-log['start_time'] == min_reins_lifetime:
            n_contracts.append(log['underwritten_contracts'][-1])
            avg_cash_left = np.mean(reins.cash_left_by_categ/reins.log['cash'][-1])
            cash_utilisation.append(avg_cash_left)

f, a = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(9,5))

a[0].hist(cash_utilisation)
a[0].set_title('Unused Cash for Reinsurers\nwho Exited ASAP')
a[0].set_xlabel('Fraction of Cash Unused')
a[0].set_ylabel('Count')
a[0].axvline(0.8, linestyle='--', color='red')


a[1].hist(n_contracts, bins = range(20))
a[1].set_title('Final number of contracts for\nReinsurers who Exited ASAP')
a[1].set_xlabel('Number of Contracts')
a[1].set_ylabel('Count')
a[1].axvline(2, linestyle='--', color='red')
plt.show()








Figure 6: Examination of why so many reinsurers exit the market so quickly. The red dashed lines indicate the bound the code uses to determine if the firm should exit. If Fraction of Cash Unused exceeds 0.8 for 48 time steps, the firm exits, or if the Number of Contracts is less than 2 for 48 time steps, the firm exits.





This is surprising, because most reinsurance requests actually don’t get fulfilled, so you would expect these reinsurers to be able write enough business to make it worthwhile to not leave the market:


Code
ts = np.arange(0, T-t_transient-1)
f, a = plt.subplots()

# subsampling for easier plot reading
ss = 30

ys = logs['added_reinrisks'][:-1]
a.plot(ts[::ss], ys[t_transient::ss], color='red', label='Requests for Reinsurance')
ys = logs['reinrisks_underwritten_at_start_of_t'][1:]
a.plot(ts[:-1:ss], ys[t_transient::ss], color='blue', label='Reinsurance Policies Created')
a.set_title('Most Reinsrisks do not get underwritten')
a.set_ylabel('Count')
a.legend()
plt.xticks(year_ticks, year_labels)
a.set_xlabel('Time (years)')
plt.show()
print(f"Probability of a reinrisk getting underwritten = {sum(logs['reinrisks_underwritten_at_start_of_t'])/sum(logs['added_reinrisks']):.2f}")








Figure 7





Probability of a reinrisk getting underwritten = 0.21


This suggests that reinsurers don’t start with enough capital to issue reinsurance; they see requests but can’t fulfill them.
Some fixes could be:

Increase the deductible on reinsurance contracts, therefore making them cheaper and more likely to get underwritten
Allow multiple reinsurers to take different layers of each reinsurance contract so the increase in capital requirement from each policy is smaller
Currently, each reinsurance request gets seen by exactly 1 reinsurer, who is chosen at random. This could be changed to only send reinsurance requests to reinsurers who could actually underwrite them (determined using a quick rule of thumb, like “is the reinsurer’s cash more than 5 times the maximum loss on the reinsurance contract?”). This would also help large reinsurers because large requests don’t get sent to tiny reinsurers.

Focusing on reinsurers who actually experienced a claim, let’s look at loss ratios:


Code
net_loss_ratios = []
total_net_claims = 0
total_net_premiums = 0
for reinsurer in sim.reinsurancefirms:
    log = reinsurer.log
    if 'claim_out' in log and log['end_time'] != None:
        res = log_to_time_series(log)
        claims = sum(res['claim_out'])
        premiums = sum(res['premium_in'])
        net_loss_ratios.append(claims/premiums)
        total_net_claims += claims
        total_net_premiums += premiums
industry_net_loss_ratio = total_net_claims/total_net_premiums
plt.hist(net_loss_ratios, bins=np.arange(min(net_loss_ratios),max(net_loss_ratios)+1, step=0.2))
plt.title('Histogram of Reinsurer Loss Ratios')
plt.xlabel('Loss Ratio')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.axvline(1, linestyle='--', color='red')
plt.show()
print(f"Minimum Loss Ratio = {min(net_loss_ratios):0.4f}")
print(f"Mean Loss Ratio = {np.mean(net_loss_ratios):0.2f}")
print(f"Maximum Loss Ratio = {max(net_loss_ratios):0.1f}")
print(f"Fraction of Reinsurers who are profitable = {np.mean(np.array(net_loss_ratios) < 1):0.2f}")
print(f"Industry Net Loss Ratio = {industry_net_loss_ratio:0.2f}")








Figure 8





Minimum Loss Ratio = 0.0584
Mean Loss Ratio = 2.62
Maximum Loss Ratio = 14.4
Fraction of Reinsurers who are profitable = 0.32
Industry Net Loss Ratio = 1.02


So reinsurance is rarely profitable, but is quite close to breaking even as an industry. Looking at Figure 5, probably the few strongly uptrending firms skew the industry loss ratio to close to 1, a number unrepresentative of the reinsurance sector as a whole.
Given the outlier with a loss ratio of 14, other similar runs could probably show a profitable reinsurance industry. Either way, this extreme variability probably means no one would want to set up a reinsurance business here.
The points I made above about reducing the number of firms who immediately exit would in my opinion also make reinsurers’ experiences more stable, but the fundamental point is that there are only 4 risk regions, so reinsurers are very un-diversified.
Reinsurers are often global and diversify across many different lines of business, so we would need a much bigger simulation with many different types of uncorrelated claims to reproduce a realistic reinsurance sector.

title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
Bankruptcy Risk
One thing I will explore in this article is whether insurers hold enough capital to cover the \(99.5^{\text{th}}\)-percentile of losses. The simplest way to model this is to imagine that each insurer independently has a probability \(p\) of going bankrupt each time step. Then if there are \(O_t\) firms operational at the start of a time step, the number of bankruptcies \(B_t\) will be distributed as \(B_t\sim\text{Binom}(O_t,p)\).
Considering each time step as an independent observation, the maximum likelihood estimator of \(p\) is then \(\sum(B_t)/\sum(O_t)\), which the following code computes:


Code
n_ins_bankrupt = 0
for ins in sim.insurancefirms:
    if ins.log['start_time'] >= t_transient and ins.log.get('dissolution reason') == 'record_bankruptcy':
        n_ins_bankrupt += 1
p_ins_bankrupt = n_ins_bankrupt/sum(logs['total_operational'][t_transient:])
p_ins_bankrupt_yearly = 1-(1-p_ins_bankrupt)**12

n_reins_bankrupt = 0
for reins in sim.reinsurancefirms:
    if reins.log['start_time'] >= t_transient and reins.log.get('dissolution reason') == 'record_bankruptcy':
        n_reins_bankrupt += 1
p_reins_bankrupt = n_reins_bankrupt/sum(logs['total_reinoperational'][t_transient:])
p_reins_bankrupt_yearly = 1-(1-p_reins_bankrupt)**12

print(f"Yearly bankruptcy chance for insurers = {100*p_ins_bankrupt :.3f}%")
print(f"Yearly bankruptcy chance for reinsurers = {100*p_reins_bankrupt :.3f}%")


Yearly bankruptcy chance for insurers = 0.014%
Yearly bankruptcy chance for reinsurers = 0.025%


Which are both safely lower than the target of 0.5%. This is surprising though, because for every firm, they underestimate the risk in one of the regions by a factor of 2, so you would think a large catastrophe there would have a decent chance of bankrupting them. However, a safety margin of 2 is built into the capital requirement calculations, defined in the isleconfig file which specifies all the parameters for the simulation:

isleconfig.py
simulation_parameters={
    ...
    "riskmodel_inaccuracy_parameter": 2,
    "riskmodel_margin_of_safety": 2,
    ...
    }

Their goal is to estimate the impact of over-reliance on a few risk models, so it seems to me a misstep to set the margin of safety equal to the riskmodel inaccuracy, because at worst it means insurers are estimating risk accurately and in the other regions overestimate it by a factor of 4. Also it makes some VaR estimates greater than the value of each house:


Code
# Take this firm because it has no reinsurance
ins = sim.insurancefirms[415]
print(f"Insurer ID: 415")
print(f"Reinsurance contracts across regions:\n        {ins.category_reinsurance}")

# Estimate VaR exactly as they do in MetaInsuranceOrg.iterate:
underwritten_risks = [{"value": contract.value, "category": contract.category, 
                       "risk_factor": contract.risk_factor, "deductible": contract.deductible, 
                       "excess": contract.excess, "insurancetype": contract.insurancetype, 
                       "runtime": contract.runtime
                       } for contract in ins.underwritten_contracts if contract.reinsurance_share != 1.0
                       ]
expected_profit, acceptable_by_category, cash_left_by_categ, var_per_risk_per_categ, ins.excess_capital = ins.riskmodel.evaluate(underwritten_risks, ins.cash)

print(f'99.5%-ile of claims per house across regions:\n        {[round(x,1) for x in var_per_risk_per_categ]} (house value = 1000).')


Insurer ID: 415
Reinsurance contracts across regions:
        [None, None, None, None]
99.5%-ile of claims per house across regions:
        [3857.9, 964.5, 3857.9, 3857.9] (house value = 1000).


Since these quantities (var_per_risk_per_categ) are directly used in determining how many new policies to write, insurers are very overcautious (only when they don’t have reinsurance, see Figure 15).

title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
Households (“Risks”)
The InsuranceSimulation object has as an attribute a list of all dictionaries, one for each house. These dictionaries are created by the following line in the InsuranceSimulation constructor:
self.risks = [{"risk_factor": rrisk_factors[i], 
               "value": rvalues[i], 
               "category": rcategories[i], 
               "owner": self} 
               for i in range(self.simulation_parameters["no_risks"])]
where:

risk_factor is the probability that, given a catastrophe hits this house’s region, the house is affected. These seem to be disabled by default (i.e. all \(=1\)), and some of the VaR calculations implicitly assume the risk factors are all \(1\) (more on this in the VaR sections).
value is the house’s value, which are all \(1000\).
category is the peril region: 0, 1, 2 or 3.
owner is the person who buys insurance. In this paper, all the policyholders are taken to part of an economy that isn’t modelled; premiums are paid from a giant pool of money which is also where insurers pay dividends into. The owner is self here because the InsuranceSimulation object holds this money pool (simulation.money_supply). When insurers ask for reinsurance they will create “reinrisks”, whose owner will be the insurer themselves.

title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
Insurance Contracts and Pricing
If an insurer underwrites the house, this dictionary is moved to the insurer, wrapped in a InsuranceContract object, and stored in insurer.underwritten_risks.
By default there are \(20\,000\) houses spread over \(4\) risk regions (called categories in the code). There are parts of the code that let them have a value, \(v\), and for insurance policies to have a limit \(L\) (they call this an excess in the paper) and a deductible, \(Q\).
As mentioned above all the house values are hard-coded to 1000, and it seems that they always use \(L=v\) and \(Q=0\) (these are the defaults, and when an insurancecontract object is created it there is no way to not use the default).
Without deductibles or limits, each claim is just \(vD\), where \(D\) is the beta-distributed with mean \(C\), the catastrophe severity. If the number of claims from a given contract is \(N\), the total claim \(S\) (ignoring time value of money) from an insurance contract is
\[
S = \sum_{i=1}^NX_i = \sum_{i=1}^NvD_i = v\sum_{i=1}^ND(C_i)
\]
where \(i\) runs over the catastrophes that occur during the policy duration \(T\), and \(X_i\) is the corresponding claim (risk factors are all \(1\) so every catastrophe leads to a claim). Because the time between catastrophes is exponentially distributed with rate \(\lambda\), \(N \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda T)\). So \(S\) has a compound Poisson distribution, and the expectation of total claims from a policy is:
\[
E[S] = vE[N]E_C[E_{D}[D|C]] = v(\lambda T)E[C]
\] Where \(v=1000\), \(\lambda = 3/100 \text{ year}^{-1}\), \(T = 1 \text{ year}\) and \(E[C] = 0.4\).


Code
v = 1. # easier than 1000
rate = 0.03 # per year
duration = 1 # year
exp_cat_size = sim.damage_distribution.mean() # = 0.4
fair_premium = v*rate*duration*exp_cat_size
fair_premium_marked_up = fair_premium*(1+s['simulation_parameters']['norm_profit_markup'])
print(f'Fair Premium = {fair_premium:0.1f}')


Fair Premium = 0.0


So the fair premium is \(1.2\%\) of the house’s value. This gets marked up by a factor of \(1.15\) for profit, to \(1.38\%\), and multiplied by a factor ranges from 0.85 to 1.2 and decreases with how well capitalized the insurance industry is.
Insurers all charge the same premium, despite having strongly disagreeing risk models. What a particular insurer would view as as fair premium for each region should be the above value of \(0.012v\) multiplied by their risk model’s inaccuracy value for that region, leading to either \(0.024v\) or \(0.006v\). So insurers have a kind of cognitive dissonance, where the premium they are charging is greatly different from what they think it should be:


Code
plt.plot(range(15000), logs['market_premium'][5000:])
plt.ylim(0, 0.0305)
plt.axhline(fair_premium_marked_up*1.2, linestyle='--',color='black')
plt.text(0,fair_premium_marked_up*1.2+5e-4, 'Market Premium Upper Bound')
plt.axhline(fair_premium_marked_up*0.85, linestyle='--',color='black')
plt.text(0,fair_premium_marked_up*0.85+5e-4, 'Market Premium Lower Bound')
plt.axhline(fair_premium_marked_up*2, linestyle='--',color='red')
plt.text(0,fair_premium_marked_up*2+5e-4, 'What Overestimating Insurers want to charge for a premium')
plt.axhline(fair_premium_marked_up*0.5, linestyle='--',color='red')
plt.text(0,fair_premium_marked_up*0.5+5e-4, 'What Underestimating Insurers want to charge for a premium')
ticks = [0.005*y for y in range(7)]
plt.yticks(ticks, [f"{y*100}%" for y in ticks])
plt.ylabel('Total Premium (% of house value)')
plt.xticks(year_ticks, year_labels)
plt.xlabel('Time (years)')
plt.title('Market Premium Over Time and\nWhat Insurers Should Want to Charge')
plt.show()








Figure 10: The time series is the actual premium charged in insurance contracts, which goes up when the total capital in insurance goes down.





This might be why they have commented out portions of code that compute the expected profit from potential new policies: if insurers considered this when underwriting they would only underwrite risks where they greatly underestimate potential claims.
This seems to be a flaw in the paper: if insurers disagreed with each other so much in expected values of risks, they would quickly realise something was wrong. To me it is more plausible that the risk model inaccuracy we should consider here only manifests when calculating upper quantiles of aggregate claims, e.g. somewhere in the tail of the risk distribution, or perhaps in incorrect correlations between different parts of an insurers portfolio. In any case it should be hard to spot and wouldn’t show up in expected values of risks.

title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
Reinsurance Contracts
For this simulation, all reinsurance policies are aggregate excess of loss, cover all of the insurer’s the policies that then exist in one region, have a deductible chosen uniformly at random from \(25\%\) to \(30\%\) of the total insured value, and have no limit. To be precise, if \(n_C\) catastrophes hit the reinsured region, and the reinsurance policy covers \(n_H\) houses, then the total claim the reinsurer will have to pay is:
\[
S = \max(0,\sum_{i=1}^{n_C}\sum_{j=1}^{n_H}(vD_{ij}) - Q)
\]
Where \(v\) is the house value, \(D_{ij}\) is the damage inflicted by the \(i\)th catastrophe on the \(j\)th house and \(Q\) is the deductible.
Because the catastrophe size \(C\) is lower bounded by \(0.25\), it is possible to have a deductible that basically guarantees a reinsurance claim on any catastrophe. Here’s a Monte Carlo simulation of catastrophes hitting a region with 100 houses, and histograms of the net claims an insurer would have to pay:


Code
n_houses = 100
house_value = 1
n_sim = int(1e5)
deductible_frac = 0.3
deductible = deductible_frac*n_houses*house_value

Cats = sim.damage_distribution.rvs(n_sim).reshape((-1,1))
Ds = scipy.stats.beta(1, 1/Cats-1).rvs((n_sim, n_houses))
agg_claims = np.sum(Ds, axis=1)
agg_claims_after_reins = np.fmin(deductible, agg_claims)

f, axes = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(9,5))

axes[0].hist(agg_claims, density=True)
axes[0].set_xlim(0,100)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Insurance Payout')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Density')
axes[0].set_title('Cost to an Insurer from a Catastrophe\nWithout Reinsurance')

axes[1].hist(agg_claims_after_reins, density=True)
axes[1].set_xlim(0,100)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Insurance Payout')
axes[1].set_title('Cost to an Insurer from a Catastrophe\nWith Reinsurance')

plt.show()








Figure 11





From the right graph, it looks like reinsurance here transfers nearly all the risk to the reinsurer. This may be the cause of the large difference in profitability - compare their loss ratios (Figure 4 versus Figure 8).
The probability of making a reinsurance claim given there was a catastrophe is:


Code
p = np.mean(agg_claims > deductible)
print(f'Probability of XOL reinsurance being triggered with highest possible deductible (30%) = {p:0.3f}')
p = np.mean(agg_claims > 25)
print(f'Probability of XOL reinsurance being triggered with lowest possible deductible (25%) = {p:0.3f}')


Probability of XOL reinsurance being triggered with highest possible deductible (30%) = 0.679
Probability of XOL reinsurance being triggered with lowest possible deductible (25%) = 0.940


My impression is that reinsurers typically want aggregate-excess-of-loss contracts to only be rarely triggered, so the choice of deductible is probably much too low.
Insurers buy reinsurance via the line actual_capacity = self.increase_capacity(time, max_var_by_categ) in the MetaInsuranceOrg.iterate method, which eventually creates the following dictionary containing the information the reinsurer gets about the risk:
risk = {"value": total_value, # sum of the covered houses' values
        "category": categ_id, 
        "owner": self, # owner is who pays the premiums, here the insurer
        "insurancetype": 'excess-of-loss', 
        "number_risks": number_risks,
        "deductible_fraction": self.np_reinsurance_deductible_fraction,
        "excess_fraction": self.np_reinsurance_excess_fraction,
        "periodized_total_premium": periodized_total_premium, 
        "runtime": 12,
        "expiration": time + 12, 
        "risk_factor": avg_risk_factor}
If a insurer wants to buy reinsurance, they create a “reinrisk” which is given to the central insurancesimulation object, and then the next time step a reinsurer will underwrite it. This means that the insurer’s capacity is not yet affected, and the insurer will create reinrisks for all regions without reinsurance if it is not meeting its capacity target, even if it would meet its capacity target from only 1 or 2 more reinsurance contracts.
If insurers are already meeting their capacity target, they will still buy reinsurance if market premiums are higher than premiums for the contracts it has already written, i.e. if the capacity boost allows them to write more profitable business.

title: Agent Based Modelling of the Insurance Industry
text:
Reinsurance Pricing
To price reinsurance, typically we would compute the expected value of claims (\(S\) in the previous subsection) and then mark it up slightly. From what I can work out, reinsurance premiums here are always 30% of the premiums the insurer receives for the same portfolio:
\[
\text{Reinsurance Premium} = 0.3 \cdot (vn_H \cdot \lambda T\cdot E[C]\cdot 1.15) \cdot \text{RMF}
\]
Where:

\(0.3\) is the “reinsurance premium share”. They don’t explain why they use 30% and this is definitely aggregate XOL reinsurance, not proportional reinsurance (all reinsurance contracts here have ReinsuranceContract.insurancetype == "excess-of-loss")
\(v\) is the value of a single house
\(n_H\) is the number of covered houses
\(\lambda TE[C]\) is the fair premium for an insurance contract covering one house
1.15 is a markup for profit

\(vn_H \cdot \lambda T \cdot E[C] \cdot 1.15\) is the premium the insurer receives for the underlying portfolio, not including the factor for how well capitalized the insurance sector is

\(\text{RMF}\) is the Reinsurance Markup Factor. It is between 0.7 and 1.35 and decreases with the total capital in the reinsurance sector

I reconstructed the above method by unfurling the call stack from MetaInsuranceOrg.process_newrisks_reinsurer, in particular the per_value_reinsurance_premium quantity and how it gets used in the ReinsuranceContract object that gets created just after. To check if I’m correct, I compute this for each of reinsurer 85’s contracts and plot against the actual premium value stored in those contracts:


Code
# A firm with a load of contracts active at the end of the simulation:
reins = sim.reinsurancefirms[85]

def predict_periodized_premium(rc):
    reinsurance_premium_share = 0.3
    v = rc.value / 1000 # number of houses
    market_reinpremium = logs['market_reinpremium'][rc.starttime]
    total_premium = reinsurance_premium_share * market_reinpremium * v 
    # periodized_premium = total_premium / runtime
    return total_premium

preds = [predict_periodized_premium(rc) for rc in reins.underwritten_contracts]
actuals = [rc.periodized_premium * 12 / 1000 for rc in reins.underwritten_contracts]

plt.scatter(actuals, preds)
plt.xlabel('Actual Total Premium (units of house value)')
plt.ylabel('Reconstructed Total Premium (units of house value)')
plt.title('A Reconstruction of Their Method of Pricing Reinsurance Contracts')
plt.xlim(0)
plt.ylim(0)
plt.axline((0,0), slope=1, linestyle='--')

plt.show()








Figure 12





Which shows that my method is close to correct but not the method they actually use (and I haven’t been able to figure out why). In my defence, they don’t explain in the code or in the paper how they price reinsurance.
To see if their method of pricing is accurate, I need to the compute the expected value of claims:
\[
E[S] = E[\max(0,\sum_{i=1}^{n_C}\sum_{j=1}^{n_H}(vD_{ij}) - Q)]
\]
over the number of catastrophes that occur, the size of those catastrophes and the house damages from each catastrophe. The following function computes this:


Code
def compute_reins_premium(n_houses, n_sim = int(1e4), deductible_frac = 0.3):
    house_value = 1
    
    deductible = deductible_frac*n_houses*house_value

    mu = 100/3*12 # 33.3 year average cat separation 
    # Discretizing a Poisson process for t << mu. P(no event) = exp(-t/mu), P(1 event) = 1-exp(-t/mu)
    p = 1-np.exp(-1/mu)
    # Sample catastrophe times
    C_times = scipy.stats.binom(1, p).rvs(n_sim*12)
    # Generate n years of damages for each region:
    C_damages = sim.damage_distribution.rvs(n_sim*12)
    # Multiply to only use damages when there was a cat
    Cs = C_times * C_damages
    # 1st index is realisations, 2nd is months
    Cs = np.reshape(Cs, (n_sim, 12))

    claim_realisations = np.zeros(n_sim)
    for year in range(n_sim):
        Cats = Cs[year, :]
        if sum(Cats) > 0:
            Cats = Cats[Cats > 0]
            Ds = scipy.stats.beta(1, 1/Cats-1).rvs((n_houses, len(Cats)))
            claim_realisations[year] = np.sum(Ds)

    # what_ins_pays = np.fmin(claim_realisations, deductible)
    claim_realisations = np.fmax(0, claim_realisations-deductible)
    prem = np.mean(claim_realisations)
    return prem

def compute_reins_premium_theirs_pure(n_houses):
    # reconstructed method without the markup factors 1.15 or RMF and 
    # with house value = 1
    reinsurance_premium_share = 0.3
    v = 1 # house value = 1
    runtime = 12
    total_premium = reinsurance_premium_share * sim.norm_premium/1.15 * n_houses
    return total_premium


The next cell computes my reconstructed reinsurance premiums, and a Monte Carlo computation of premiums for portfolios with deductibles of \(25\%\), \(30\%\), and 1 to 300 houses (I don’t run the following cell here because it takes 8 minutes):
houses = range(1, 301)
prems = {
     0.25:[compute_reins_premium(x, n_sim = int(2e4), deductible_frac = 0.25) for x in houses],
     0.3:[compute_reins_premium(x, n_sim = int(2e4), deductible_frac = 0.3) for x in houses]
     "their_way": [compute_reins_premium_theirs_pure(x) for x in houses]
     }
I can now compare my reconstruction of their method to a full Monte Carlo computation:


Code
# load the output of the previous cell:
with open('data/reinsurance_pricing.pkl', 'rb') as file:
    prems = pickle.load(file)

houses = range(1,301)
plt.plot(houses, prems[0.25], label='Deductible = 25%')
plt.plot(houses, prems[0.3], label='Deductible = 30%')
plt.plot(houses, prems['their_way'], label='Their Way')
plt.legend()
plt.xlabel('Number of Houses')
plt.ylabel('Reinsurance Premium (units of house value')
plt.title('Reinsurance Premium as a function of Number of Houses\nand Deductible')
plt.show()








Figure 13





Which shows that their method is surprisingly good - perhaps there is a reason why their computation makes sense that I don’t understand. (Their method is certainly much faster, and the simple claims generating process in this model is probably what makes a method like theirs possible.) However, for low reinsurance deductibles, their premium is too low:


Code
# Average the ratio to smooth Monte Carlo variation:
x = np.mean(np.array(prems[0.25])/np.array(prems['their_way']))-1
print(f"At a deductible of 25%, their premium should be {100*x:0.0f}% higher")


At a deductible of 25%, their premium should be 28% higher


Which surely contributes to the unprofitability of reinsurers (industry loss ratio of 1.02).

title: The Interpretation of Probability Theory
text:
Sometimes articles/books/people say that probabilities have an objective existence, sometimes they say that they just measure our uncertainty.
When analysing data, the methods we use and therefore the insights we draw and decisions we make, depend on what we think a probability represents. The prevailing interpretation of quantum mechanics is that when you measure a system, there are many possible results of that measurement, each with a given probability that we can calculate.
Therefore the meaning of probabilities has both commercial and profound implications, so in this article I briefly explain my position, and hope to move you slightly towards it. There are of course many points I could expand upon, and many issues not touched on here, but I want to keep this to a less than ten minute read.
Articles/books/people don’t usually explicitly state their interpretation of probability, but from what I can tell the most common interpretation of a probability is as a long term frequency: if you repeat a trial a large number of times, the probability of an event represents the limiting frequency of that event, as the number of trials tends to infinity. This means probabilities describe a property of the system in question and are to be estimated as best we can.
In so far as the universe is deterministic, exactly repeating a trial will give exactly the same result, making long term frequency 1 for the inevitable result and 0 for all other outcomes. It seems that for the long term frequency view to make sense we need some non-determinism (fundamental randomness) in each trial, or that the trials are not exactly repeated (so that variation in initial conditions gives the variation in outcome).
Consider tossing a coin. A coin spinning through the air and landing on a table is a fully determined physical system, so if we know the initial position, velocity, orientation, angular velocity and friction with the table it lands on, there are differential equations we can solve that will exactly predict how it will land; there is nothing random about each trial.
So it would be possible to design a machine to predictably toss a coin, and with this machine we could choose any long term fraction of the tosses that result in heads. Nobody would call this coin tossing random any more, so it seems that it is the lack of knowledge/control over the precise initial conditions that result in us calling human coin tosses random. The same can be said for dice rolls, and (if we control the precise details of the shuffling) drawing cards from a deck.
Many scientists take the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, which states that the results of measurements of extremely small objects (molecules and smaller) are non-deterministic. This an on-going debate however, with many scientists taking the many-worlds view, which is fully deterministic. Also, what about free will - are our minds purely a function of our brains, which are themselves deterministic systems? If not, could free will be the source of randomness which limits our abilities of prediction to long term frequencies?
My point is not to take a stance on the interpretation of quantum mechanics or the existence of free will, but to draw attention to the fact that if we say something is “fundamentally random”, or that exactly repeating a trial could give a different outcome, we are actually taking a stance on some very difficult philosophical/scientific issues. Surely we don’t have to make our minds up about this in order to interpret the statement “this policyholder has a 5% chance of making a claim in the coming year”?
Everyone is happy to talk of the probability of a dice roll, because it is in the future, undetermined (unless the universe is deterministic, in which case future dice rolls are determined). But when outcomes are already fixed but just unknown, most sources in my experience would not speak of the probability of the conceivable outcomes. This comes up mostly in the inference of parameters - the parameter is the same in each trial so it is fixed but unknown. Indeed, from a pure maths perspective only random variables (functions) can have probability densities, not parameters (just real numbers).
But this seems to be sadly restrictive - it certainly would be useful to quantify our uncertainty in propositions that are determined but unknown. Confidence Intervals (CIs) are used to solve this kind of problem, but in my opinion they have a very awkward interpretation. We have to learn to avoid saying what we really want to say (“the parameter of interest has a 95% probability to be in a certain range”) and say instead that “the procedure we used to calculate the CI will result in an interval containing the true value 95% of the time” (which is surely a statement about the universe: if you repeat the experiment, the long term frequency will take a certain value).
Pure maths (from my reading of Wikipedia, textbooks, lecture courses) seems to most strongly align with the long term frequency view of probability, usually justified by the law of large numbers. This is because it immediately follows from the law of large numbers that:
The issue is that you have to already know what probabilities are to interpret what “converges, with probability 1” means. This has a well-defined, abstract notion within the maths, but mapping it to a non-abstract concept requires thinking from outside mathematics.
Probabilities representing long term frequencies are clearly consistent here (the theorem is almost true by definition from this view), but this is a reason for using normed measure theory for modelling long term frequencies, not evidence that repeated trials will have stable long term frequencies.
The main rules of probability theory, like \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)P(B|A)\), were well known long before it was axiomatised. Indeed, this is a definition (of conditional probability) in pure maths, not a deduction (and therefore carries no information). This suggests there is something that just makes sense about the rules of probability that allows them to be divined without axiomatic basis by people like Pascal and Fermat; they just work for the kinds of problem they were addressing.
I see pure maths as reverse engineering those already existing rules by coming up with the minimal assumptions that imply those rules (or equivalently, the most general objects that satisfy them). This is clearly useful, but the question remains: why do we have those rules to begin with? Are long term frequencies the only entities that satisfy rules like \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A \text{ and }B)\)?
I became convinced of a particular interpretation of probability theory when I read Probability Theory: The Logic of Science by E. T. Jaynes (Jaynes 2003). In it, he starts from the question: how can we we be precise about our degree of confidence in a proposition? Formal logic is very useful when we can be perfectly sure of whether propositions and implications are true or false, but how should we think if we aren’t perfectly sure? Jaynes lays down three rules that this new theory of plausibility must satisfy:
Using numbers allows us to be precise, and defines an order: by convention he takes more confident degrees of belief to be represented by larger numbers.
Humans make inferences and predictions all the time without knowing probability theory, and Jaynes claims that we use the following (progressively weaker) rules:
If a cold causes sneezing and we observe sneezing, then we become more confident that this person has a cold. Someone having committed a crime makes it more likely that their fingerprints are at the crime scene; if we learn that the defendant’s fingerprints are at the crime scene, we become more suspicious. In both cases it’s not clear by how much more confident we should get - intuitively it depends on whether there could be another explanation for the observed fact - and it’s the question of “by how much more confident?” that this theory is intended to answer.
When you make an inference, it’s a fun exercise to test in your mind whether the way you update your beliefs can be mapped onto one of the above rules.
One thing to note here is that how plausible something is very much depends on the relevant information you have: two perfectly rational people may wildly disagree on how plausible something is, simply because they have seen different evidence. (Although, if they learn that a rational person strongly disagrees with them, this is new information which would cause them to update their beliefs.)
Therefore it only makes sense to talk about the plausibility of a proposition \(A\) in the light of some specified information, \(I\); \(\pi(A)\) doesn’t make sense, only \(\pi(A|I)\).
From those three rules (and several lectures’ worth of reasoning), you can derive the following rules that must be satisfied for any valid set of plausibilities for any group of propositions \(A,\ B,...\) in the light of any particular information \(I\):
In other words, exactly the rules of probability theory. There are of course many more details, but the main result is that if you are doing probability theory, you are also doing plausibility theory.
Because the derivation of plausibility theory is completely indifferent as to why you are uncertain, it can be used to model any kind of uncertainty, be it from the free will of others, from physical non-determinism, or from ignorance.
